entry.title: HMAC-Signed Webhooks: Securing Your Event Stream
entry.summary:
HMAC-Signed Webhooks: Securing Your Event Stream
Webhooks are powerful—they let external systems react to your events in real time. But there's a catch: how do you know the webhook actually came from you? Enter HMAC signatures. When your system sends a webhook to a third party's endpoint, anyone who knows that URL can fire requests at it, impersonating your service. They could trigger false transactions, corrupt data, or worse. HMAC (Hash-Based Message Authentication Code) lets you cryptographically sign each webhook with a shared secret: You and the webhook consumer share a secret key (known only to both) You compute an HMAC-SHA256 hash of the webhook body using that secret You send the hash as a header (usually X-Signature or X-Webhook-Signature) They recompute the hash on their end—if it matches, the webhook is authentic Signature = HMAC-SHA256(webhook_body, shared_secret) Send as: X-Signature: sha256=<hex_encoded_signature>
The consumer verifies by computing the same hash and comparing it to the header value. A mismatch means tampering or forgery. No secrets travel over the wire (only the computed hash) Proves both authenticity (it came from you) and integrity (it hasn't been modified) Standard crypto, widely supported across languages and frameworks HMAC-signed webhooks are the lightweight, battle-tested way to make your event stream trustworthy.
